title: One-dimensional motion with constant acceleration
explanation:
Constant acceleration means velocity changes by the same amount every second: $v=v_0+a\,t$. Many real motions can be described this way using their average acceleration [1], and a motion whose acceleration changes sharply can be split into parts, each with its own constant acceleration [2].

Displacement needs one more idea. When acceleration is constant, velocity changes linearly, so the average velocity is just the simple average of the initial and final velocities [3], $\bar v=\frac{v_0+v}{2}$. Then $\Delta x=\bar v\,t$. Substituting $v=v_0+a\,t$ gives the workhorse equation $\Delta x=v_0\,t+\tfrac12 a\,t^2$.

Signs matter. Pick a positive direction first; a velocity or acceleration pointing the other way is negative. A car braking while moving forward has a negative acceleration.
keyIdeas: Choose a positive direction before writing any signs.

workedExample.problem: A scooter moving at $1$ m/s speeds up at $4$ m/s² for $3$ s. Find its final speed and displacement.

pitfalls: Using $\Delta x=v\,t$ with the final speed, which overestimates when the object is speeding up.
Dropping signs: a slowing object has acceleration opposite its velocity.

citations.quote: Furthermore, in many other situations we can describe motion accurately by assuming a constant acceleration equal to the average acceleration for that motion.
